solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Drops one outside entrance of Institute North East for a bit of culture

definitions.note: plural answer; 'a bit of culture' means one branch of it, but the fine arts are taken as a single field

parts.note: to drop one is slang for breaking wind

indicators.note: the entrance of a word is the way in, its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone breaks wind at the door of a northern arts institute, a crude joke about culture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops one' reads as a verb and its object; together they are a single slang phrase, and the insertion goes in after the very first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine arts, painting, sculpture and the like, are the core of what is meant by culture.

clue.text: Sweet innocent thing, Blair (excluding that is reduced unemployment benefit)

indicators.note: excluding leaves the named letters out of the name

parts.note: CHERIE Blair, wife of the former Prime Minister, without IE (i.e. = that is)

indicators.note: a phrase reduced to its bare minimum is cut down to its initials

parts.note: unemployment benefit cut down to its initials

explanation.surface: A jibe that Blair is a sweet innocent, set beside a complaint about cuts to the dole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blair' is not Tony but his wife Cherie; take the IE out of her name.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is a chubby angelic child in art, the stock image of sweet innocence.

clue.text: Leader who's climaxed, one lacking in metal

indicators.note: the metal is lacking the one, so it goes without it

explanation.surface: A sneer at a party leader who has had his fun and lacks any backbone of steel.
explanation.walkthrough: David Cameron was the Conservative Prime Minister when this ran; 'in metal' tells you where the missing one is found.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Cameron led the Conservative Party and the country.

clue.text: Things agreed informally: removing head of penis does something

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, and removing it cuts that letter off

parts.words: Things agreed informally: removing head of penis
parts.note: PACTS, informal agreements, losing P, the first letter of penis

explanation.surface: A lurid sentence about an informal agreement and a circumcision.
explanation.walkthrough: The head of the word penis is just its first letter, P, taken off PACTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to act is to take action rather than sit still.

clue.text: Brewed IP Ale, rot — it won't put hairs on your chest

definitions.text: it won't put hairs on your chest

indicators.note: brewing stirs ingredients together into something new

explanation.surface: A beer snob dismisses a rotten IPA as too weak to put hairs on your chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put hairs on your chest' is said of strong drink, which the surface leans on; an epilator does the opposite and removes hair.
explanation.definitionFit: An epilator is a device that pulls out body hair, so it certainly won't put any on your chest.

clue.text: Naff Sun squeezing one divorcee of no particular gender

indicators.note: to squeeze something is to hold it tight inside
naff means rubbish, so the paper's name comes out botched

explanation.surface: A dig at the naff Sun newspaper running a story on a divorcee.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid, and naff is British slang for tacky; the capital S disguises a three-letter anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Unisex means suitable for either sex, so of no particular gender.

clue.text: UK security service crap — was way off target

parts.note: MI, Military Intelligence, as in MI5 and MI6

explanation.surface: A rant that British intelligence is crap and got it badly wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The security service is only MI, not MI5 or MI6: the number is left off.
explanation.definitionFit: Mishit is its own past tense, and to mishit is to strike a ball badly, so way off target.

clue.text: In whose films the actors swear sailor ain't no Rocky

definitions.text: In whose films the actors swear

indicators.note: rocky means shaky and unsteady, so the letters wobble out of place

explanation.surface: Film talk: a foul-mouthed sailor is no Rocky Balboa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocky' looks like Stallone's boxing film, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Quentin Tarantino's films are famous for their characters' relentless swearing.

clue.text: Crown squeezed by one single mobster

indicators.note: whatever is squeezed by something is pressed inside it

parts.note: a cap is a crown, as on a tooth

explanation.surface: A lone gangster crushing a crown, as if seizing power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One single' reads as a single idea, but it is two words for two chunks, and the enumeration (2,6) hides where the crown goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Al Capone was the most notorious Chicago gangster.

clue.text: Drop behind a human dynamo

parts.note: a tear is a drop, as in teardrop

explanation.surface: An instruction to fall back behind an unstoppable go-getter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop behind' reads as a single phrase meaning fall back; split it into two nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear-arse is British slang for a restless, hyperactive person, a human dynamo.

clue.text: Piss, holding pint — get it everywhere

indicators.note: the slash holds the pint the way a hand holds a glass, around it

parts.note: a slash is British slang for a pee
the first letter of pint standing in for the word

explanation.surface: A drunk at the urinal, pint in hand, spraying everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Slash as a noun for urinating is everyday British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To splash is to scatter liquid about, getting it everywhere.

clue.text: (& 14ac.) Archer's duty: extraction of a bigger share of income from wealthy types

definitions.text: extraction of a bigger share of income from wealthy types

parts.note: the legendary outlaw archer of Sherwood Forest who took from rich people to give to poor ones
a duty is a levy, the three-letter sort the state charges on income

explanation.surface: A question of what duty an archer owes, answered with robbing the rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer' tempts you towards Jeffrey Archer, the novelist and peer; it is Robin Hood, who stole from the rich to give to the poor.
explanation.definitionFit: The Robin Hood tax was a campaign for a levy on financial transactions to take more from banks and the wealthy.

clue.text: Badly missed squeezing belly and Stalin's thing

indicators.note: to squeeze something is to hold it tight inside
done badly, the word comes out wrong, its letters muddled

explanation.surface: Someone badly missed hugging a pot-bellied Stalin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly missed' reads as sorely longed for; the adverb is the anagram signal. 'Thing' is loose slang for someone's speciality.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalin was the archetypal despot, so despotism was his thing.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Dealer in spirits? Three parts pissed but elegant with it

indicators.note: three parts of a five-letter word means keeping only three of its letters

parts.note: the last three letters of TIPSY (pissed)

explanation.surface: A drinks dealer who is three sheets to the wind yet still stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' and 'pissed' point at booze; the dealer trades in ghosts. Only three of TIPSY's five letters are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A psychic deals with the spirits of the dead, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Screwing around with male, Tina's good

definitions.text: Screwing around with male, Tina's good

indicators.note: screwing twists something round, so TINA gets twisted

explanation.surface: Tina is having a good time sleeping around with a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwing around' looks like the definition, but 'around' is also C, circa; the whole clue describes Tina's cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes Tina being unfaithful with another man, which is cheating.

clue.text: Fanny just wouldn't be seen wearing one

definitions.text: Fanny just wouldn't be seen wearing one

parts.note: the surface reads a woman's name; really British slang for the vulva
the surface reads she'd never be seen in one; really her fanny is only just hidden by it

explanation.walkthrough: Fanny reads as a woman's name, but in British slang it is the vulva, which a G-string only just covers.
explanation.definitionFit: A G-string is so skimpy that the wearer's fanny is only just hidden.

clue.text: Not a justification for ordering sex on cue

indicators.note: ordering the letters puts them into a new order

explanation.surface: Demanding sex on cue is not justifiable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordering' reads as demanding, but it means putting the letters in a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse is a justification offered, so saying there is none is a plain synonym phrase.

clue.text: Cyclops would have one in the morning with popular murderous buffoon

parts.note: the setter Cyclops speaking of himself: I'd, I would

explanation.surface: The one-eyed Cyclops of myth would have one eye open at dawn beside a jolly killer.
explanation.walkthrough: Cyclops is the setter's name, so 'Cyclops would' is the setter saying I'd; the one-eyed giant of myth is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Idi Amin, Uganda's dictator, killed thousands and was mocked for his clownish antics.

clue.text: (& 21ac.) The Broadway play, film, and TV series, showing an occasional shag?

definitions.text: Broadway play, film, and TV series

parts.note: odd = occasional, as in the odd drink
to couple is to have sex, to shag

explanation.surface: A show billed as having the odd bit of sex in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' does double duty as the start of the title; shag is British slang for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Simon's The Odd Couple was a Broadway play, then a film, then a TV series.

clue.text: Pisspoor attempt to outflank anti-smokers

indicators.note: to outflank is to get round both sides

parts.note: ASH, Action on Smoking and Health, the UK anti-smoking campaign

explanation.surface: A feeble effort to get round the anti-smoking lobby.
explanation.walkthrough: ASH is a British charity campaigning against smoking.
explanation.definitionFit: Pisspoor is coarse slang for worthless, and trash is worthless stuff.

clue.text: see 20ac.
Spot member stuck into mound

indicators.note: something stuck into a heap ends up inside it

explanation.surface: A body part pushed into a heap, with a double meaning on member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' tempts as a limb or worse; it is an MP.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though 'spot' also means a place, which the surface of a mound leans on.

clue.text: French place that's the end of Cameron? "— 'e 'asn't adapted"

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter
adapted means altered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mock-Cockney jeer that Cameron, dropped in France, hasn't adapted.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped aitches leave just E, A, S, N, T to rearrange; the apostrophes count for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a city in western France.

clue.text: House after smarmy Osborne starts is a seedy place?

indicators.note: the starts of the two words are their first letters

parts.note: the first letters of smarmy Osborne

explanation.surface: A jab that George Osborne, the smarmy Chancellor, keeps a house in a seedy district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' is a placement word, so the chunk that comes first in the clue goes second in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is the London district long known for sex shops and strip clubs, hence seedy, with a question mark for the generalisation.

clue.text: "Queer", "butch" am I? That's uncalled-for

indicators.note: queer in its old sense of odd, so the letters come out strangely

explanation.surface: Someone bristles at being labelled queer or butch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queer' reads as one of the labels, but it means odd, and applies to the next three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A remark that is a bit much goes too far, so is uncalled-for.

clue.text: During bonk, name something that tops head almost — port

indicators.note: almost the word stops just short, losing its last letter
what happens during something falls within it

parts.note: bonk and shag are both British slang for sex
HAIR, which tops the head, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A bedroom scene: during sex, name the thing on top of your head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'During' comes first but governs the name, which goes inside the bonk; the port is left as the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Shanghai is China's great seaport.

clue.text: Stubborn as the Democrats, symbolically

definitions.meaning: like a donkey, the Democratic Party's symbol

explanation.walkthrough: The US Democratic Party's symbol is a donkey, so symbolically the Democrats are like a mule.
explanation.definitionFit: Mules are famously obstinate, so mulish means stubborn; a mule is half donkey, close enough to the Democrats' emblem.
